text: Large Language Models, or LLMs, are computer programs trained to understand and generate human-like text. They work by predicting the next word in a sentence based on patterns learned from massive amounts of data, such as books, articles, and websites. This training data helps them recognize grammar, facts, and even some reasoning. To get useful answers, users practice prompt engineering—writing clear, specific instructions or questions. For example, asking “Summarize this article in three bullet points” works better than a vague request. LLMs are impressive: they can write essays, translate languages, and answer trivia. However, they have limits. They may produce incorrect “facts” confidently, and they lack true understanding or emotions. They also cannot access real-time information unless connected to live tools. So, while helpful, they should be used with careful checking.
